query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Imposing a surface mechanical treatment (e.g., shot peening or UNSM) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will produce an ultrafine‐grained surface layer that, upon high‐temperature exposure in air, promotes the in-situ formation of a dense, adherent native oxide scale (primarily HfO2 and ZrO2). This protective layer will significantly slow oxygen ingress without degrading the alloy’s bulk mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast, as-produced equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy with its inherently coarse surface microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface mechanical treatment (e.g., shot peening or ultrasonic nanocrystal surface modification) to induce a nanocrystalline/ultrafine-grained surface layer.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in static air at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours; mechanical loading tests (tensile/compressive) at room temperature and elevated temperatures with strain rates in the range of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: The ultrafine-grained surface layer increases the nucleation density of protective oxides and limits fast oxygen diffusion paths along coarse grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The high density of refined grains and associated high-angle boundaries accelerates the formation and consolidation of a thin, continuous oxide scale (mainly HfO2 and ZrO2) that acts as a diffusion barrier. Because the surface-modified layer is thin relative to the bulk, the internal microstructure—and thus the excellent yield strength and ductility—is preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the treated specimens will exhibit a much slower weight gain during oxidation (indicative of improved oxygen resistance) while retaining similar room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and elevated-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Untreated cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which develops a poorly adherent, non-protective oxide and exhibits rapid oxygen penetration during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under controlled isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C in air and may not translate directly to environments with significantly different oxygen partial pressures, thermal cycles, or when the treatment parameters inadvertently alter bulk residual stress levels.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work on ultrafine-grained AlCoCrFeNi HEAs (e.g., PMC9026100 evidence on oxidation kinetics and oxide scale formation) and mechanical performance studies on HfNbTaTiZr (e.g., PMC7514121 evidence) suggest that grain refinement can enhance oxidation protection without compromising strength, it remains uncertain whether similar protective oxide chemistry (HfO2/ZrO2) will form in HfNbTaTiZr. Moreover, the optimal parameters (e.g., peening intensity, treatment duration) for this alloy are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of cast HfNbTaTiZr samples. Treat one batch with the selected surface mechanical process (with well-defined shot peening/UNSM parameters), leaving the other as untreated control. Expose both batches to isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. Post-exposure, perform cross-sectional microscopic analysis (SEM/TEM) and weight gain measurements to assess oxide scale density and thickness. Conduct room-temperature and elevated-temperature tensile/compressive mechanical tests on both sets.
measurements: Weight gain per unit area (mg/cm²) after oxidation
Oxide scale microstructure and thickness (via SEM/TEM)
Room-temperature tensile ductility (%) and yield strength
High-temperature (1000 °C) yield strength under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanically treated samples do not show a substantial reduction (e.g., >30% lower weight gain) in oxidation or if their mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) deteriorate by more than ~10% compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that surface mechanical refinement confers improved oxygen resistance without sacrificing performance is falsified.

Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. Thus, there is a need to develop advanced materials with superior surface oxidation resistance and improved mechanical properties at high temperature. High entropy alloys (HEAs) represent an emerging class of advanced materials for high temperature applications owing to their promising mechanical properties, namely, outstanding structural strength, high hardness,, enhanced fracture toughness, prominent fatigue resistance, and remarkable oxidation and corrosion resistance. The oxidation behavior of HEAs has been extensively reported. Kim et al. examined the oxidation behavior of a Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni HEA system for a duration of 24 h at three different temperatures, 900, 1000, and 1100 °C, revealing mass gain of 1.76, 4.45, and 9.08 mg/cm2, respectively. Nong et al. studied the high temperature oxidation behavior of AlCrFeNiTiMnx (where x = 0 and 0.5) HEAs at 900 °C for 100 h and probed the poor oxidation resistance of Mn containing alloys, which was attributed to the adverse effect of Mn-rich oxides. In a diffusion controlled phenomenon, a linear regression model was fitted using Arrhenius curves. The slope of the curve yields the value of −Ea/R in the temperature range of 850–1050 °C, which was utilized to calculate the value of activation energy. The slope of the curves indicates that the activation energy is the lowest value for the as-cast sample while it is highest for the SFP_1800 sample, indicating the high oxidation resistance of the latter. The possible reason for the higher activation energy for the processed samples is the highly stable nature of the thin oxide layer formed on these samples (discussed in the next section).
